title: WTA Finals headed to Charlotte from 2027; tour moves headquarters there too
dek: The WTA announced Charlotte will host the Finals from 2027 through 2029 at Spectrum Center, the home of the NBA's Hornets. The tour will relocate its global headquarters from St. Petersburg, Florida to Charlotte. The move ends six hosts in seven years and gives the WTA operational control of its marquee event for the first time.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: The WTA Finals will move to Charlotte, North Carolina for 2027-2029 with the tour's headquarters relocating there as well, ending a cycle of six different hosts in seven years.
bottom_line: The tour's ability to achieve its stated financial targets and sustain the five-day format without player conflicts will determine whether Charlotte anchors the WTA Finals or marks another waypoint in a cycle of instability. The precise prize money and revenue terms for 2027 onward have not been announced.
body:
The WTA will host its Finals in Charlotte, North Carolina from 2027 through 2029, ending a seven-year run of instability that saw six different host cities and marking the first time the tour will operate the event rather than license it to an external promoter.
The Finals will be held at Spectrum Center, home of the NBA's Hornets, according to ESPN's reporting. The tour's global headquarters will relocate from St. Petersburg, Florida to Charlotte as well, per BBC Sport.
Prior to this announcement, the WTA Finals had moved between Guadalajara, Fort Worth, Cancun, Riyadh and Shenzhen in rapid succession. A planned 10-year arrangement in Shenzhen lasted one year. Riyadh had been set to host for a third consecutive Finals in November 2026, but the arrangement ended one year early after the WTA and Saudi Tennis Federation mutually agreed to conclude the hosting agreement, per ESPN's reporting.
The instability reflected several pressures: geopolitical tensions between the United States and Iran, the waning interest of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund in sports sponsorship (which also led the fund to halt bankrolling of LIV Golf), and disappointing attendance at recent Finals venues. BBC Sport reported that crowds have often been disappointing.
WTA chair Valerie Camillo stated that the tour had always owned the Finals but lacked operational control. "We're taking control of the creation of the revenues and the controlling of the expenses and the delivery of the entire thing. And that allows us to control our own destiny," Camillo said, according to ESPN. The shift represents a move away from the licensing fee model that had relied on outside promoters to organize the event.
The tournament will be shortened from eight days to five, due to the Hornets' NBA schedule and frequency of home games. Camillo said the WTA has begun exploring alternative formats with players, but acknowledged that if the round-robin structure survives, finalists would need to play every day, per BBC Sport.
Financial pressures underscore the move's urgency. The Telegraph, cited in ESPN's reporting, estimates the WTA is poised to reach $23 million in operational losses this season and would have only $15 million on hand by year's end. Camillo said in a statement that "2026 is a year of transition for the WTA. We are doing the normal belt tightening you would expect of any business while also absorbing the unexpected cost of relocating the WTA Finals to Indian Wells."
Camillo framed the Charlotte deal as a pathway to stability and growth. "What's most important to know is that we have a clear path to deliver consistent sustainable financial performance in 2027 and beyond supported by strong revenue and audience growth," she said, per ESPN. The deal came together in less than six months following a competitive global selection process, ESPN reported.
Spectrum Center has hosted tennis exhibition events for the past two seasons, per ESPN.
